title: How I Made a Chatbot With My Knowledge: Turning My Technical Articles into a GraphRAG Assistant
subtitle: As software engineers, our personal blogs and notes often end up as chronological archives — hundreds of Markdown files, JSON payloads, and code repositories scattered across years of work. Traditional vector search (standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG) helps find keywords and paragraphs, but it fails when a query requires understanding how disparate technical decisions link together across an entire ecosystem.

content.html: As software engineers, our personal blogs and notes often end up as chronological archives — hundreds of Markdown files, JSON payloads, and code repositories scattered across years of work. Traditional vector search (standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG) helps find keywords and paragraphs, but it fails when a query requires understanding how disparate technical decisions link together across an entire ecosystem.

To solve this, I transformed my archive into an interconnected Knowledge Graph and built a GraphRAG architecture assistant. Here is the step-by-step technical journey of how I structured the data, extracted entities and hyperedges, computed semantic similarities, and wired everything to an LLM.

content.alt: How I Made a Chatbot With My Knowledge: Turning My Technical Articles into a GraphRAG Assistant

content.text: 1. The Challenge: Transforming Unstructured JSON into Documents

content.html: My blog archive (src/data) contained raw JSON files spanning article dumps, GitHub project repositories, video records (YouTube/Aparat), and author metadata:

content.code:
src/data/
├── aparat-videos.json
├── github-projects.json
├── posts/
│   ├── Real-Time-Data-Ingestion-Kafka-to-ClickHouse.json
│   └── ...
├── profile.json
└── youtube-videos.json

content.html: When feeding raw .json files into AST-based code parsers (like Graphify), the engine classified them as source code rather than semantic documents, resulting in zero nodes.
To resolve this, I built an automated transformer script (build_kg_docs.py) to convert all JSON records into clean, structured Markdown documents with explicit headers and frontmatter:
This formatted 525 documents into an /md staging directory, ready for semantic extraction.
Using graphify routed through an OpenAI-compatible proxy (api.avalai.ir/v1) using gpt-5.6-luna, I extracted semantic entity-relation-entity triples and multi-component system hyperedges:

content.code:
env $(cat .env | xargs) graphify extract ./md --backend openai --model gpt-5.6-luna
env $(cat .env | xargs) graphify cluster-only ./md --backend openai --model gpt-5.6-luna

items: Total Entities & Nodes: 426 nodes
Total Directed & Semantic Edges: 353 relationships (93% extracted, 7% inferred)
Topic Communities Detected: 111 distinct architectural clusters grouped via the Leiden algorithm

content.html: The resulting graph.json uncovered the core pillars of my technical writing:

items: ClickHouse & Streaming Ingestion (9 direct connections)
Retrieval-Augmented Generation & Vector Stores (12 connections)
Fine-Grained Authorization (Keycloak & OpenFGA) (10 connections)
Modular Go Architecture (Clean Architecture, Uber FX, SQLC) (10 connections)

content.html: To make this graph usable in my web frontend (a TanStack Router blog), I needed to compute the similarity between articles.

Initially, applying standard Jaccard similarity across shared neighbors resulted in false positives: unrelated posts that shared only a single broad concept like #Machine Learning received a similarity score of 1.0.
To fix this, I implemented an Adamic-Adar / Inverse-Degree Weighted Similarity algorithm in Python:

content.alt: How I Made a Chatbot With My Knowledge: Turning My Technical Articles into a GraphRAG Assistant

content.html: If two articles shared a rare technical concept (such as ClickHouse Kafka Engine with 2 edges), it provided a high score; if they shared an umbrella tag with 24 edges, the weight approached zero. This generated clean, high-confidence mappings for my site's related_posts.json.
Standard RAG searches for direct text similarity, but real software architecture questions are multi-hop. For example:
“How does the streaming Kafka ingestion pipeline handle deadlocks and schemas when inserting into ClickHouse?”
A standard vector database might return a snippet about Kafka or a snippet about ClickHouse. GraphRAG, however, traverses the structural path:

content.alt: How I Made a Chatbot With My Knowledge: Turning My Technical Articles into a GraphRAG Assistant

content.html: I built graph_rag.py to ingest graph.json, perform Breadth-First Search (BFS) graph expansion from seed entities, and provide the extracted subgraph to the LLM:

content.code:
import os, json, requests
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import List, Dict, Any

GRAPH_JSON_PATH = "./md/graphify-out/graph.json"
OPENAI_BASE_URL = os.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", "https://api.avalai.ir/v1")
OPENAI_API_KEY = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
MODEL_NAME = os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-5.6-luna")


class GraphRAGRetriever:
    def __init__(self, graph_path: str):
        with open(graph_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            data = json.load(f)
        self.nodes = {n["id"]: n for n in data.get("nodes", [])}
        self.adjacency = defaultdict(set)
        self.hyperedges = data.get("graph", {}).get("hyperedges", [])
        for link in data.get("links", []):
            self.adjacency[link["source"]].add(link["target"])
            self.adjacency[link["target"]].add(link["source"])

    def traverse(self, seeds: List[str], depth: int = 2, max_nodes: int = 15):
        visited = set(seeds)
        queue = [(s, 0) for s in seeds]
        while queue and len(visited) < max_nodes:
            curr, d = queue.pop(0)
            if d >= depth:
                continue
            for neighbor in self.adjacency.get(curr, []):
                if neighbor not in visited:
                    visited.add(neighbor)
                    queue.append((neighbor, d + 1))
        return [self.nodes[nid] for nid in visited if nid in self.nodes]


def query_graph_rag(user_query: str):
    retriever = GraphRAGRetriever(GRAPH_JSON_PATH)
    seeds = [nid for nid, n in retriever.nodes.items() if n.get("label", "").lower() in user_query.lower()]
    subgraph_nodes = retriever.traverse(seeds or ["concept_clickhouse", "concept_kafka"])
    context = "\n".join([f"- {n['label']} ({n.get('file_type')}): {n.get('rationale', '')}" for n in subgraph_nodes])
    prompt = f"""Use the following knowledge graph context to answer the architectural question:
Context:
{context}
Question: {user_query}"""
    res = requests.post(
        f"{OPENAI_BASE_URL.rstrip('/')}/chat/completions",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {OPENAI_API_KEY}"},
        json={"model": MODEL_NAME, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
    ).json()
    return res["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

content.html: In the frontend router (/blog/$slug), I connected the graph mapping to a normalized slug resolver to guarantee resilient fuzzy matching across hash suffixes (-530ff573762f) and index identifiers (--17):
By converting flat articles into an interconnected Knowledge Graph and GraphRAG engine:

items: Interactive Navigation: Readers see genuinely related posts based on shared architectural topology rather than simple keyword collisions.
Context-Aware Chatbot: An AI assistant that understands the relationships between my Go workers, Kafka pipelines, and ClickHouse databases.
Auditing Knowledge Gaps: The graph immediately surfaced 256 isolated concepts and thin communities, giving me a clear roadmap of which deep-dive articles to write next.

content.code:
$ python3 graph_rag.py
=== GraphRAG Architecture Assistant (Type 'exit' or Ctrl+C to quit) ===

content.text: Ask a question: How can we design a software architecture capable of handling 100,000 requests per second (high TPS)? Please explain the key architectural components and strategies involved.

content.html: — — Traversing Graph & Querying deepseek-v4-flash — -
— — Model Response — -

To architect for 100,000 requests per second (100k RPS), you cannot rely on a monolithic, synchronous request/response cycle. The bottleneck will shift from application logic to data persistence, distributed coordination, and observability. Based on the architectural patterns and documented pipelines in the knowledge graph, you need a decoupled, event-driven, layered system that aggressively offloads work from the hot path.
Here is the comprehensive blueprint, mapped to the specific documented components:
At 100k RPS, you must intercept and filter traffic before it hits your origin servers.

items: Component: Cloudflare Workers for Edge Request Handling. Deploy serverless Workers at the edge to handle CORS, request routing, proxying, and lightweight authentication (e.g., API key validation). This absorbs the bulk of invalid or pre-flight requests, drastically reducing the load on your core API services.

Strategy: Strategy Design Pattern. Use this in the edge logic to isolate routing/sorting algorithms (e.g., geographic routing vs. tenant-based routing) so you can swap traffic-shaping logic without redeploying the entire origin stack.

content.html: Your application tier must be stateless to scale horizontally with a load balancer.

items: Component: Layered Clean Architecture (Go Web API). Structure the core services strictly into Model, Repository, Service, Controller, and DTO layers. This prevents code duplication and reduces coupling, allowing each microservice to be independently scaled and deployed. Repositories are isolated, so the database driver can be swapped without impacting the service logic.

Pattern: CQRS Microservices Architecture. Split the read and write paths. For 100k RPS, reads vastly outnumber writes. CQRS allows you to scale the read models independently (using caching) and the write models (using queues), preventing database contention.

Pattern: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Dependency Inversion. Apply DDD to enforce dependency inversion, particularly for billing and critical transactions (e.g., Stripe). Keep the core domain logic pure and independent of infrastructure, ensuring high throughput and testability without I/O blocking.

content.html: Direct synchronous database hits will cap your throughput well below 100k RPS. You must use a multi-tier data access strategy.

items: Pattern: High-Scale Data Processing (Redis + Async DB). Implement the High-Traffic Click Application Design. All incoming requests write to Redis first (in-memory, sub-millisecond latency) and read from Redis for immediate consistency. Do not hit the primary database (e.g., PostgreSQL) on the request thread.

Pattern: Database-per-service Isolation. Strictly enforce database-per-service. A shared database is a distributed lock and a single point of failure — it creates coupling, resource contention, and ambiguous ownership, which will cause cascading failures at 100k TPS. The graph explicitly recommends isolation to prevent this.

Component: Flat Columnar KPI Architecture. For any analytics or KPI aggregation (e.g., dashboard reads), use ClickHouse with flat columns instead of JSON blobs. This allows vectorized aggregation and columnar storage to read only specific counters, which scales far better than parsing nested data on the fly.

content.html: To handle the write volume and offload heavy processing, use a Fire-and-Forget + Event-Driven architecture.

items: Component: Kafka ClickHouse Ingestion Pipeline (High-Scale Framework).

content.html: — Writes Path: The API layer pushes the event to Kafka (or a similar log-based queue). Kafka acts as a massive buffer that absorbs write spikes.
— Reads Path: Redis remains the source of truth for immediate reads; Kafka replicates to ClickHouse for historical queries.

items: Pattern: Poller–Dispatcher–Worker Architecture. Once events hit Kafka, use a Poller to batch-pull messages, a Dispatcher to route them to bounded worker queues, and separate Worker pools to process side-effects (e.g., email, report generation, database aggregation). This isolates error domains — if one worker fails, it only backs up its bounded queue, preventing cascading failure across the system. Support graceful shutdown and independent scaling for these workers.

content.html: AuthN/AuthZ must not be a bottleneck. Implement OAuth2/OIDC + fine-grained permissions.

items: Component: Keycloak and OpenFGA Authorization Architecture. Use Keycloak for centralized OIDC token issuance (this is a heavy operation, do it rarely — use token caching). Use OpenFGA (Google Zanzibar pattern) for highly scalable, distributed, fine-grained authorization checks. OpenFGA is designed for low-latency, high-fanout relationship checks, which is critical at 100k RPS.

content.html: At this scale, “unknown” is the real killer. You need complete visibility and rapid deployment.

items: Component: Go OpenTelemetry Observability Guidance. Instrument every request using OpenTelemetry tracing (spans). Integrate this with Sentry to map traces to transactions and spans for automatic error tracking and latency bucketing. This is non-negotiable for diagnosing downstream bottlenecks in Redis, Kafka, or DBs.

Component: Architectural Optimization of Shared Sandbox Deployments (GitLab CI/CD). Implement isolated, ephemeral sandbox environments for performance testing and parallel deployment. Use GitLab CI/CD with matrix builds to test the 100k RPS load against separate stacks, ensuring zero regression before rolling out to the main fleet.
Request hits Cloudflare Worker (edge). CORS/Auth filtered.
Controller (Layered Clean Arch) parses the request and validates shape.
Service uses Strategy Pattern to select the handler.
Redis is hit immediately (GET/SET). If cache hit, respond immediately (90%+ of requests).
If write: Event pushed to Kafka. Redis is updated optimistically. Response returns 200 to the client in < 5ms.
Poller-Dispatcher-Worker consumes Kafka, updates the primary Database-per-service (Postgres) asynchronously.
ClickHouse ingests flattened logs via CDC/Kafka for analytics.
OpenFGA validates permissions only for non-cached resources.
OpenTelemetry tags the trace, and Sentry tracks the event.

content.html: This architecture is successful because it eliminates synchronous I/O from the request path. Redis absorbs the heat, Kafka buffers the write burst, and ClickHouse accelerates analytics. Every component scales independently, and the graph patterns dictate strict data possession and asynchronous data flows — which is precisely how you breach the 100k RPS threshold.
